extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators and researchers (university instructors and scholars in mathematics education)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and improving how undergraduate mathematics majors read, comprehend, and are taught mathematical proofs (focus on beliefs, responsibilities, and pedagogical implications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification responsibility (Belief #1)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a good proof, every step is spelled out for the reader. The reader should not be left wondering where the new step in the proof comes from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey items contrasted this belief with the alternative: 'When reading a good proof, I expect I will have to do some of the work to verify the steps in the proof myself.' Empirical finding: 75% of mathematics majors preferred the explicit-justification statement, while most mathematicians preferred the alternative. Example/anti-pattern: Students expecting all details explicitly leads to passivity and failure to construct sub-proofs; mathematicians typically expect readers to fill in some inferences and do sub-proofs themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as step-by-step justification (Belief #2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I can say how each statement in a proof follows logically from previous statements, then I understand the proof completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was presented as a single-statement survey item. Majority of mathematics majors (75%) agreed with this notion whereas the majority of mathematicians (67%) disagreed. Contrasting view: mathematicians view understanding as also including explanation of why theorems are true, the structure and methods of the proof, and ability to use the ideas in new contexts. Example measures of understanding used in interviews: ability to reproduce the proof, explain it to someone else, or identify overarching methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time investment for comprehension (Belief #3)
rubrics_metrics.description: How long should you typically spend reading a proof that is presented to you in your classes (in minutes)? — mathematics majors often expect short times (mean min 17, mean max 20), while mathematicians expect longer (mean min 30, mean max 37).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey asked open-response times; many majors gave ≤15 minutes as typical maximum. Mathematicians often expect 15 minutes to two hours for undergraduate-length proofs. Implication: students underestimate time required and may not engage in necessary extended study (constructing sub-proofs, drawing diagrams, checking examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram/drawing responsibility (Belief #4)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading a good proof, if a diagram can help my understanding, it should be included. I should not be expected to draw a diagram myself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey contrasted this with the alternative that students expect sometimes to draw diagrams themselves. Majority of majors (66%) preferred statement A (diagrams should be included), while many mathematicians expected students to sometimes draw diagrams. Example: quartic-polynomial argument where students who resolved confusion often drew a graph; most did not draw graphs even when they noted it would help. Pedagogical implication: mismatch between teacher expectations and student behavior can hinder comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of proof: explanation vs conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should not be merely formal demonstrations for conviction; they should explain why theorems are true, systematize mathematical theories, discover new mathematics, and facilitate communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on de Villiers and subsequent education literature: proofs in classroom should promote understanding by explaining why, not just providing formal demonstration. Empirical note: students (and some teachers) may see primary purpose as providing conviction; this limits engagement with the explanatory/communicative roles of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of detail in presented proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide the amount of explicit logical detail to include: excessive detail can mask important conceptual ideas; too little detail may leave students unable to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians differ in what inferences they deem 'obvious' and what students should supply. Some argue that adding pedagogical steps improves clarity; others claim it reduces pedagogical quality by encouraging passivity. Instructors should balance clarity and prompting active reader work. Evidence: prior study found mathematicians divided on whether adding an algebraic step improved pedagogical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader active-engagement practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading a proof productively requires active practices: writing marginalia, constructing sub-proofs, checking examples, drawing diagrams, and decoding mathematical shorthand with a pencil in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematician interview excerpts emphasize substantial reader work (writing sub-proofs, checking examples, drawing pictures). Teaching implication: students should be encouraged/taught to adopt these practices because authors often leave such work for readers intentionally to promote understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as social/interactional accomplishment
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument becomes a proof after the social act of accepting it as a proof; proof status depends on community scrutiny and audience participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from Manin and Devlin emphasize that proving is interactional: both prover and audience participate in constructing and validating arguments. Pedagogical implication: reading proofs involves social/interpretive work, not merely passive reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different epistemic purposes for student vs presented proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs students write (for assessment) focus on form and explicit correctness; proofs presented by professors aim to communicate insights and methods and therefore may omit some low-level detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because students rarely read peers' proofs or expect proofs to be communicative, they may generalize from assessment-focused experiences and expect all steps to be explicitly justified. Instructional recommendation: make students aware of the differing purposes and give opportunities to use proof as a communicative tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for assessing arguments (study rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating mathematical arguments participants were asked three criteria: Did they feel they understood the argument? Did they find the argument convincing? Did they think the argument constituted a mathematical proof?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three axes were used in the qualitative study of 28 undergraduates who evaluated ten arguments. Observed student behavior: tended to accept invalid arguments, read superficially, focus on calculations and stepwise justification rather than higher-level structure. Use of these three evaluation criteria can be an assessment rubric for studies of proof comprehension/validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness (and potential drawbacks) of alternative proof formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative formats for presenting proofs (e.g., structured proofs, generic proofs, more transparent forms) have been proposed to increase comprehension but existing quantitative studies show little benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors suggest a reason: making aspects of a proof more transparent may reduce reader active engagement, causing some students to take a less active role and thus diminish comprehension. Recommendation: refining students' beliefs about their responsibilities may be required in addition to format changes.
